news.title: A shared force frame improves a robot hand's removal tasks
news.summary: A University of York team and partners studied a three-finger hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Across six tasks, adding fingertip pose and wrist-frame forces raised mean success from 24% to 83%.
news.details: Researchers at the University of York, with colleagues in Edinburgh, Jena and King's College London, posted a paper on November 11 about DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand for detaching adhered objects, cleaning surfaces and retrieving obscured targets. Each fingertip measures force along three axes. To compare readings as the fingers bend, the authors transform them into a shared coordinate frame attached to the wrist. Each force direction is then described relative to the same reference rather than a differently oriented finger.
news.technical_novelty: A University of York team and partners studied a three-finger hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Across six tasks, adding fingertip pose and wrist-frame forces raised mean success from 24% to 83%. Each control program learns from 20 successful demonstrations collected through human operation. It receives three camera views, joint states and selected fingertip observations. Across six core tasks, mean success rose from 24% with cameras and joint information alone to 83% when fingertip position and orientation, along with forces expressed in wrist coordinates, were added. That comparison changes several inputs together; intermediate configurations help examine their contributions. Three further scenarios were evaluated with the full configuration. The paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Robotics, a research journal.
news.engineering_impact: A University of York team and partners studied a three-finger hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Across six tasks, adding fingertip pose and wrist-frame forces raised mean success from 24% to 83%. The technical contribution concerns representation of contact. A sensor on a bending finger turns with it, so the same physical force can yield different local components. Transforming the readings using joint geometry removes that ambiguity before the neural network receives them. Camera and joint inputs, demonstrations and evaluation procedures remain fixed when input configurations are compared. Actions execute at 15 hertz, meaning fifteen updates per second; average policy-computation latency was 23.5 milliseconds with a standard deviation of 4.1 milliseconds.
news.limitations: A University of York team and partners studied a three-finger hand for detaching objects and cleaning surfaces. Across six tasks, adding fingertip pose and wrist-frame forces raised mean success from 24% to 83%. The mechanical setup bounds the result: the hand is positioned in advance, its wrist pose is fixed and a linear stage supplies vertical movement. The authors identify whole-arm positioning and larger-workspace operation as further integration work, beyond the evaluated local separation tasks.
news.evidence_status: Author-run experiments; accepted by IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Input comparisons cover six core tasks; independent reproduction is not established here.
news.organization: University of York; University of Edinburgh; Friedrich Schiller University Jena; King’s College London
news.body:
Researchers at the University of York, with colleagues in Edinburgh, Jena and King's College London, posted a paper on November 11 about DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand for detaching adhered objects, cleaning surfaces and retrieving obscured targets. Each fingertip measures force along three axes. To compare readings as the fingers bend, the authors transform them into a shared coordinate frame attached to the wrist. Each force direction is then described relative to the same reference rather than a differently oriented finger.

Each control program learns from 20 successful demonstrations collected through human operation. It receives three camera views, joint states and selected fingertip observations. Across six core tasks, mean success rose from 24% with cameras and joint information alone to 83% when fingertip position and orientation, along with forces expressed in wrist coordinates, were added. That comparison changes several inputs together; intermediate configurations help examine their contributions. Three further scenarios were evaluated with the full configuration. The paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Robotics, a research journal.

The technical contribution concerns representation of contact. A sensor on a bending finger turns with it, so the same physical force can yield different local components. Transforming the readings using joint geometry removes that ambiguity before the neural network receives them. Camera and joint inputs, demonstrations and evaluation procedures remain fixed when input configurations are compared. Actions execute at 15 hertz, meaning fifteen updates per second; average policy-computation latency was 23.5 milliseconds with a standard deviation of 4.1 milliseconds.

The mechanical setup bounds the result: the hand is positioned in advance, its wrist pose is fixed and a linear stage supplies vertical movement. The authors identify whole-arm positioning and larger-workspace operation as further integration work, beyond the evaluated local separation tasks.

news.title: 112 robot tasks receive difficulty levels under one protocol
news.summary: A National University of Singapore team and partners introduced ManiLadder's simulated tasks in four levels. Difficulty is assigned using one reference model with the same demonstration count and training schedule.
news.details: A team including the National University of Singapore posted ManiLadder on November 12, a study introducing 112 simulated object-manipulation tasks organized into four difficulty levels. The collection covers rigid and deformable objects, one or two arms, simple grippers and multi-finger hands. The researchers want to measure not only the variety of actions a robot learns but also how demanding a task it can solve under a common learning budget.
news.technical_novelty: A National University of Singapore team and partners introduced ManiLadder's simulated tasks in four levels. Difficulty is assigned using one reference model with the same demonstration count and training schedule. Calibration gives each task 20 demonstrations and the same reference control model with fixed training settings. The model learns to reproduce demonstrated actions, and its success determines the task's level. It trains for 40,000 steps, with 50 evaluation attempts every 5,000 steps. Task conditions are revised until performance falls within the intended range. Final method comparisons also use 50 test attempts per task, with evaluation starting conditions separated from those used to collect demonstrations.
news.engineering_impact: A National University of Singapore team and partners introduced ManiLadder's simulated tasks in four levels. Difficulty is assigned using one reference model with the same demonstration count and training schedule. The reference model has 50 million trainable parameters. Its result depends on both the task and the available data, so the level is anchored to a reproducible learning procedure. The authors additionally check the difficulty structure with other models and random initializations. Final reporting weights each task equally, preventing convenient cases from dominating simply because they are repeated more often. This gives developers two distinct comparison targets: success on a task and coverage across tasks at each difficulty level. Calibration targets 60–100% reference-model success for the easiest level and 0–4% for the hardest.
news.limitations: A National University of Singapore team and partners introduced ManiLadder's simulated tasks in four levels. Difficulty is assigned using one reference model with the same demonstration count and training schedule. The levels depend on the reference learner and training budget. Comparing a new controller with the published results requires preserving demonstration counts, evaluation starting conditions and completion criteria. Changing those settings changes the measuring procedure used to assign difficulty in the first place.
news.evidence_status: An author-published research paper and evaluation protocol; the reported results were obtained by the research team.
news.organization: National University of Singapore and collaborating universities

news.title: Japan asks for clearer support for robots, components and training data
news.summary: At a November 12 meeting with manufacturers, Japan's prime minister called for concrete support for robot development and deployment. Companies requested help with production, domestic artificial-intelligence technology, data accumulation and early adoption.
news.details: Japan's prime minister Sanae Takaichi met robot and component makers on November 12 to discuss support for physical AI, artificial-intelligence systems that guide actions in the physical world. She instructed ministers to reflect company requests in the growth-strategy implementation plan and provide predictable information about support measures and required budgets. The meeting reiterated 2040 ambitions: deploying roughly 10 million AI robots and securing a global market share for Japanese industry of more than 30%, or 20 trillion yen.
news.technical_novelty: At a November 12 meeting with manufacturers, Japan's prime minister called for concrete support for robot development and deployment. Companies requested help with production, domestic artificial-intelligence technology, data accumulation and early adoption. Companies identified four needs: support from domestic robot and component research through volume production; faster development of domestic AI technologies; mechanisms for accumulating data; and multi-year support for early adoption. The government links robotics to worker shortages, physical workload and hazardous operations. The published speech assigns these issues to further planning, with specific support amounts still to be set out. A separate Sankei report published by ITmedia on November 13 corroborates the meeting and the targets.
news.engineering_impact: At a November 12 meeting with manufacturers, Japan's prime minister called for concrete support for robot development and deployment. Companies requested help with production, domestic artificial-intelligence technology, data accumulation and early adoption. For engineering teams, the requests identify connected parts of development: components, software, training data and sites where the combined system can be tested. The speech specifically calls for support spanning research and trials through production facilities. This matters to equipment planning and long projects because opportunities to gain operating experience also depend on who funds early installations and data collection. Access to a model is one dependency within that larger development process, alongside hardware availability and usable worksite information.
news.limitations: At a November 12 meeting with manufacturers, Japan's prime minister called for concrete support for robot development and deployment. Companies requested help with production, domestic artificial-intelligence technology, data accumulation and early adoption. The next practical document is the growth-strategy implementation plan, setting out support measures and required budgets. The November 12 speech does not enumerate individual engineering-program amounts or schedules; clarifying those details is the instruction given to the responsible minister.
news.evidence_status: Official policy speech corroborated by Sankei reporting; targets and instructions are presented as government plans.

news.title: Serve opens delivery commands and a simulated integration environment
news.summary: Serve Robotics introduced an interface for requesting and tracking robot deliveries. Developers can use a simulated test environment, while physical-robot access depends on operator approval and service coverage.
news.details: U.S. company Serve Robotics opened a developer portal for its sidewalk delivery-robot network on November 11. An application can request a delivery, specify collection and drop-off, and track the trip through an application programming interface, or API: a set of commands for communicating with the service. Serve also provides a test environment containing simulated robots. Documentation and this environment are available immediately; live-robot access requires company approval and service coverage at the requested location.
news.technical_novelty: Serve Robotics introduced an interface for requesting and tracking robot deliveries. Developers can use a simulated test environment, while physical-robot access depends on operator approval and service coverage. Serve reports a network of 2,000 robots across more than 150 neighborhoods in 20 U.S. cities. Dispatch, routes, navigation and operational supervision remain with the operator. Developers build services on top of that infrastructure, such as delivery for a local shop. The simulated environment allows them to test the full delivery sequence and unusual situations before using a physical machine. The network figures are company-reported, and the allocation of operating responsibilities also comes from Serve’s description.
news.engineering_impact: Serve Robotics introduced an interface for requesting and tracking robot deliveries. Developers can use a simulated test environment, while physical-robot access depends on operator approval and service coverage. The engineering boundary separates the customer's application from the operating delivery system. The application specifies work through software commands, while Serve handles movement and supervision. The test environment supports checking request sequences and unusual cases before an integration affects street operations. It is useful to assess order creation, progress updates and completion separately: they belong to one process, but an application error can arise at any stage. That is an editorial implication of the documented division of functions, rather than a published evaluation of a new application.
news.limitations: Serve Robotics introduced an interface for requesting and tracking robot deliveries. Developers can use a simulated test environment, while physical-robot access depends on operator approval and service coverage. Live-machine use has two explicit conditions: Serve approval and an address inside its service area. Integration checks therefore need to cover both the software exchange and whether the requested trip can be carried out by the operator's actual delivery network.
news.evidence_status: Official Serve release and technical explanation; network size and available functions are operator-reported.

news.title: Japan connects waste operators with robotics developers
news.summary: Japan's environment ministry is forming a consortium to introduce robots using artificial intelligence into waste processing. It will collect facility needs, technical barriers and potential partners for trials.
news.details: Japan's Ministry of the Environment announced a consortium on November 13 to support physical AI in waste management and resource recycling. Here physical AI means systems connecting artificial intelligence with machine actions at a worksite. Government bodies, municipalities, companies and industry groups are invited. The consortium aims to improve information exchange between technology suppliers and facilities seeking automation, bringing together their needs and implementation barriers.
news.technical_novelty: Japan's environment ministry is forming a consortium to introduce robots using artificial intelligence into waste processing. It will collect facility needs, technical barriers and potential partners for trials. The ministry identifies specific pressures: more complex products, growing sorting categories, worker shortages and safety requirements. Obstacles to robotics include poor communication of site needs, insufficient matching of trial partners and incomplete rules. Membership applications are open until December 3, with no membership fee. A first meeting is scheduled for December 17 in a hybrid in-person and online format. Its program includes the consortium's objectives, a presentation from the economy ministry's robotics unit and examples of work in the sector.
news.engineering_impact: Japan's environment ministry is forming a consortium to introduce robots using artificial intelligence into waste processing. It will collect facility needs, technical barriers and potential partners for trials. For developers, this concerns obtaining requirements for a particular job. Different products and sorting categories change which features a sensor must recognize and which objects a machine will handle. The announcement does not select a particular arm or algorithm; it first organizes exchange between technology builders and people who know the facility. The engineering value is an opportunity to define working conditions, trial preparation and safety requirements before equipment reaches a site. These are practical dependencies for an integration project, especially where material streams change.
news.limitations: Japan's environment ministry is forming a consortium to introduce robots using artificial intelligence into waste processing. It will collect facility needs, technical barriers and potential partners for trials. The first scheduled event is a December 17 meeting with sector examples and discussion of the consortium's objectives. Its published scope centers on needs, partner matching and rules; specifications for an individual robotic process will depend on the projects that follow.
news.evidence_status: Official ministry announcement about sector coordination; it contains no measurements of a particular robotic installation.
